source.title: Finding Alignments Between Interpretable Causal Variables and Distributed Neural Representations
source.authors: Atticus Geiger; Zhengxuan Wu; Christopher Potts; T. Icard; Noah D. Goodman

record.tranche_reason: The study uses distributed interchange interventions to measure whether task-relevant representations align with high-level variables in rotated subspaces. This bears on distributed features in language models and on their dimensionality, but it does not test the original sparse-feature superposition setup.
record.gate_note: The paper reports IIA results for learned alignments, localist and brute-force baselines, and randomly initialized networks. The main rows below are the results that bear on distributed representations or the dimensionality of aligned subspaces; the toy-network random initialization results do not test the claim versions.
record.test_reason: In fine-tuned BERT, task variables align near-perfectly with rotated (non-neuron-aligned) subspaces, while localist alignments fail. That bears on V4's claim that real language models spread features across many neurons. It does not test superposition proper (more features than dimensions), SAE features, or the minimum dimensionality of features.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct in substance. The authors also stress that the equality representations, which cannot be decomposed into input identities, show a symbolic tree-structured algorithm implemented in the network.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces DAS, learning orthogonal rotations and measuring interchange-intervention accuracy for task-specific causal variables. It does not reproduce the original sparse-feature superposition method or measure its sparsity-dependent geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: IIA varies with layer and intervention size; for example, lexical-entailment IIA is lower at Layer 7 than Layer 9 for the reported settings.

fits_no_version.finding: In a 3-layer feed-forward net trained on hierarchical equality, both equality relations align with rotated subspaces (IIA up to 1.00), versus localist 0.73 and brute-force 0.60. The equality subspace cannot be decomposed into input identities (≈0.51).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Small trained networks encode abstract task variables in distributed, non-neuron-aligned subspaces.

fits_no_version.finding: BERT's lexical-entailment subspace decomposes almost perfectly into word-identity subspaces (IIA 0.97–0.98).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Apparent relational variables in LMs can be composite data structures of simpler variables.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, volume 236, 2024; 3rd Conference on Causal Learning and Reasoning
record.problems: The language-model experiment is a task-specific fine-tuning study on MoNLI and analyzes only the CLS token. Reported table values are the best results from three rotation-training runs, without error bars or a stability analysis beyond that selection. The measurements establish successful alignments at tested subspace sizes, not minimal feature dimensionality or general LLM feature coverage.
record.rows_left_out: Other high-level hypotheses and many layer/intervention-size cells from Tables 1 and 2 are omitted because they do not add a distinct result about the tested versions beyond the reported alignment, decomposition, and layer-variation results.

untested.parts: No sparse features exceeding dimensions, no near-orthogonal overlap, no sparsity transition or geometry.
No capacity or importance account of polysemanticity.
No test of polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure.
Only BERT-base fine-tuned on MoNLI, CLS token, two binary task variables. No SAE recovery, no sparse features, no evidence of more features than dimensions.
No dictionary or SAE features studied.
Subspace size is a fixed hyperparameter (64–256 in BERT). Minimum feature dimensionality and multi-dimensional features are not assessed.

missing.what: Brute-force baseline IIA for lexical entailment (0.64 at Layers 7 and 9, 0.57 at Layer 11), the comparison showing distributed beats any localist window
Random-network control: DAS IIA stays ~0.50 in small nets but rises to 0.64 at hidden size 4096, so an expressive search can partly fit random structure
Negation plus lexical entailment model: IIA 0.96–1.00 at Layer 9 but only 0.65–0.67 at Layer 7
Learned rotations move most basis vectors; authors call the representations highly distributed

record.verdict_notes: This is a causal-abstraction method paper (DAS), not a superposition study. Distributed coding in a rotated basis is compatible with superposition but does not show it: a non-privileged basis without more features than dimensions would give the same result. Reported values are the best of three seeds, with no error bars. The reader's V6 links and the V4 limits_scope label on R4 were removed; R4 is about substructure, not V5-style SAE features.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test sparse features exceeding network dimensions, their overlap or near-orthogonality, or a sparsity-dependent transition and regular geometry.
Does not test whether limited capacity causes neuron polysemanticity or whether importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
The language-model evidence is from BERT fine-tuned on a specific NLI task and analyzes selected task variables at the CLS token; it does not test broad feature coverage in LLMs or SAE recovery.
No sparse autoencoders or claims about canonical, complete, or stable dictionary features are tested.
The study measures alignment to subspaces of specified sizes, but does not establish the minimum dimensionality of a feature or test superposition under sparse-feature capacity pressure.

relationships.condition: BERT-base fine-tuned on MoNLI, CLS token, Layers 9 and 11
relationships.reason: Distributed (rotated-basis) alignments of lexical entailment reach IIA 0.97–1.00, versus localist 0.47 and brute-force ≤0.64. So the variable is spread across neurons, not in disjoint neuron groups (R1–R3, R6, R7).
relationships.display_finding: Distributed alignments in a rotated basis captured lexical entailment with interchange intervention accuracy of 0.97–1.00, against 0.47 for localist and at most 0.64 for brute-force alignments. The variable is spread across neurons rather than held in disjoint neuron groups.

relation.reason: The study reports its own distributed-versus-localist alignment results, providing indirect evidence for V4.

tranche.reason: DAS uses learned rotations and causal interchange interventions to test distributed representations in fine-tuned BERT, bearing on V4 through a different method.

source_check.notes: Table 2 reports training-data IIA, selecting the best of three seeds; it does not quantify neuron participation or establish superposition capacity. Section 5.3 finds that the apparent lexical-entailment representation decomposes into word-identity representations; the undecomposable equality result concerns the separate feed-forward experiment.
